This post introduces a user-defined function for casting **sf** objects of class
`LINESTRING` or `POLYGON` into substrings.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| fig-cap: ""
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  error = FALSE,
  tidy = "styler",
  echo = TRUE,
  dpi = 300,
  dev = "ragg_png",
  dev.args = list(background = "#FAF8F2"),
  fig.crop = FALSE,
  out.width = "100%",
  fig.path = "assets/img/blog/"
)
library(knitr)
```

## Required **R** packages

```{r}
#| label: libs
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: ""
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

background <- "#FAF8F2"
foreground <- "#203B47"
map_title <- "inter-tight"
map_regular <- "inter"
segment_palette <- c("#335F83", "#A84742", "#287C70")

sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter Tight", family = map_title)
sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter", family = map_regular)
showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi"))
showtext::showtext_auto()

theme_set(
  theme_void(paper = background, base_family = map_regular, ink = foreground) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        family = map_title, face = "bold", size = 18, margin = margin(b = 4)
      ),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, margin = margin(b = 8)),
      strip.text = element_text(family = map_title, face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.margin = margin(12, 14, 12, 14)
    )
)
```

## The problem

The **sf** package includes [`st_cast`](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/reference/st_cast.html),
a powerful function that transforms geometries into other types of geometries
(i.e. `LINESTRING` to `POLYGON`, etc.).

```{r}
#| label: 20190505_italycast
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| tidy: styler
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Four maps of Italy show a single fill for the multipolygon, separate
#|   colors for its polygon parts, boundary lines and individual vertices.
italy <- ne_countries(country = "italy", returnclass = "sf")
italy_pol <- st_cast(italy, "POLYGON")
italy_lin <- st_cast(italy_pol, "LINESTRING")
italy_pt <- st_cast(italy_lin, "POINT")

italy_stages <- bind_rows(
  list(
    MULTIPOLYGON = st_sf(
      part_colour = "#D5E2DD", geometry = st_geometry(italy)
    ),
    POLYGON = st_sf(
      part_colour = rep_len(c("#A9BFCF", "#CEA897", "#8FB9AA"), nrow(italy_pol)),
      geometry = st_geometry(italy_pol)
    ),
    LINESTRING = st_sf(geometry = st_geometry(italy_lin)),
    POINT = st_sf(geometry = st_geometry(italy_pt))
  ),
  .id = "stage"
) |>
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = unique(stage)))

ggplot(italy_stages) +
  geom_sf(
    data = filter(italy_stages, stage != "POINT"),
    aes(fill = part_colour),
    colour = foreground, linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = filter(italy_stages, stage == "POINT"),
    colour = foreground, size = 0.65
  ) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  facet_wrap(vars(stage), ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Italy by geometry type")
```

What I missed when using `st_cast` was the possibility of breaking
`LINESTRING` objects into subsegments:

```{r}
#| label: 20190505_italycastsub
#| warning: false
#| tidy: styler
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: "Outline of Italy split into short line segments, with alternating colors distinguishing adjacent segments."
stdh_cast_substring <- function(x, to = "MULTILINESTRING") {
  ggg <- st_geometry(x)

  if (!unique(st_geometry_type(ggg)) %in% c("POLYGON", "LINESTRING")) {
    stop("Input should be LINESTRING or POLYGON")
  }
  for (k in 1:length(st_geometry(ggg))) {
    sub <- ggg[k]
    geom <- lapply(
      1:(length(st_coordinates(sub)[, 1]) - 1),
      function(i) {
        rbind(
          as.numeric(st_coordinates(sub)[i, 1:2]),
          as.numeric(st_coordinates(sub)[i + 1, 1:2])
        )
      }
    ) %>%
      st_multilinestring() %>%
      st_sfc()

    if (k == 1) {
      endgeom <- geom
    } else {
      endgeom <- rbind(endgeom, geom)
    }
  }
  endgeom <- endgeom %>% st_sfc(crs = st_crs(x))
  if (class(x)[1] == "sf") {
    endgeom <- st_set_geometry(x, endgeom)
  }

  if (to == "LINESTRING") {
    endgeom <- endgeom %>% st_cast("LINESTRING")
  }
  return(endgeom)
}
italy_sub <- stdh_cast_substring(italy_lin, "LINESTRING")
italy_sub$segment_colour <- rep_len(segment_palette, nrow(italy_sub))

ggplot(italy_sub) +
  geom_sf(aes(colour = segment_colour), linewidth = 0.65) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  labs(
    title = "Italy in subsegments",
    subtitle = "Each segment connects two consecutive vertices"
  )
```

## An approach

One way to split a line is to create a `LINESTRING` for each pair of
consecutive vertices. Here is the outline of mainland Spain before and after
splitting.

```{r}
#| label: 20190505_testspain
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| tidy: styler
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Two outlines of mainland Spain. The left panel shows a continuous line
#|   and the right panel uses alternating colors to reveal individual segments.
test <- ne_countries(country = "spain", returnclass = "sf") |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  slice_max(order_by = st_area(geometry), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING")

coordinates <- st_coordinates(test)[, c("X", "Y")]
geom <- lapply(
  seq_len(nrow(coordinates) - 1),
  \(i) coordinates[c(i, i + 1), , drop = FALSE]
) |>
  st_multilinestring() |>
  st_sfc(crs = st_crs(test)) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING")

spain_stages <- bind_rows(
  st_sf(
    stage = "Original line",
    segment_colour = foreground,
    geometry = st_geometry(test)
  ),
  st_sf(
    stage = "Individual segments",
    segment_colour = rep_len(segment_palette, length(geom)),
    geometry = geom
  )
) |>
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = unique(stage)))

ggplot(spain_stages) +
  geom_sf(aes(colour = segment_colour), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  facet_wrap(vars(stage), nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "One boundary, many segments")
```

## The function `stdh_cast_substring`

Finally, I wrapped the solution into a function and extended it a little bit:

- When the input is not a `LINESTRING` or a `POLYGON`, it returns an error and
  stops.

- The function accepts **sf** objects with several rows or `sfc` objects with
  several geometries, and returns the same class as the input. In the case of
  **sf** objects, the input `data.frame` is added.

- By default, the output is a `MULTILINESTRING` geometry. This has the benefit
  that the output has the same number of geometries as the input. This can be
  modified by setting the `to` parameter to `LINESTRING`, which only casts the
  `MULTILINESTRING` object into `LINESTRING`.

```{r}
#| label: function
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| tidy: styler
#| fig-cap: ""
stdh_cast_substring <- function(x, to = "MULTILINESTRING") {
  ggg <- st_geometry(x)

  if (!unique(st_geometry_type(ggg)) %in% c("POLYGON", "LINESTRING")) {
    stop("Input should be LINESTRING or POLYGON")
  }
  for (k in 1:length(st_geometry(ggg))) {
    sub <- ggg[k]
    geom <- lapply(
      1:(length(st_coordinates(sub)[, 1]) - 1),
      function(i) {
        rbind(
          as.numeric(st_coordinates(sub)[i, 1:2]),
          as.numeric(st_coordinates(sub)[i + 1, 1:2])
        )
      }
    ) %>%
      st_multilinestring() %>%
      st_sfc()

    if (k == 1) {
      endgeom <- geom
    } else {
      endgeom <- rbind(endgeom, geom)
    }
  }
  endgeom <- endgeom %>% st_sfc(crs = st_crs(x))
  if (class(x)[1] == "sf") {
    endgeom <- st_set_geometry(x, endgeom)
  }

  if (to == "LINESTRING") {
    endgeom <- endgeom %>% st_cast("LINESTRING")
  }
  return(endgeom)
}
```
The function could be improved in terms of performance. Given that it works at
the coordinate level, high-resolution objects introduce some delay.

```{r}
#| label: 20190505_benchmarkfunction
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| tidy: styler
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: "Map of South America with country boundaries split into short segments, illustrated with alternating colors."
test100 <- ne_countries(
  continent = "south america",
  returnclass = "sf"
) %>%
  st_cast("POLYGON")

test50 <- ne_countries(50,
  continent = "south america",
  returnclass = "sf"
) %>%
  st_cast("POLYGON")


init <- Sys.time()
t1 <- stdh_cast_substring(test100, "LINESTRING")
end <- Sys.time()
kable(end - init, format = "markdown")


init <- Sys.time()
t2 <- stdh_cast_substring(test50, "LINESTRING")
end <- Sys.time()
kable(end - init, format = "markdown")


t2$segment_colour <- rep_len(segment_palette, nrow(t2))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = test50, fill = "#E6ECE7", colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = t2, aes(colour = segment_colour), linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-94, -32), ylim = c(-58, 15), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "South America in subsegments",
    subtitle = "Natural Earth boundaries at 1:50 million"
  )
```

There is a difference in performance: `test100` has `r length(st_geometry(test100))`
polygons decomposed into `r format(length(st_geometry(t1)), nsmall=1, big.mark=",")`
substrings, while `test50` has `r length(st_geometry(test50))` polygons
decomposed into `r format(length(st_geometry(t2)), nsmall=1, big.mark=",")`
substrings. The higher-resolution outlines take longer to split because they
contain more vertices.
